title: Design a news feed
summary: Home timelines for 100 M daily users: fan-out on write versus on read, the hybrid for accounts with millions of followers, cursor pagination and a k-way merge.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** users follow other users. The home feed shows recent posts from the people you follow, newest
first, and loads fast.
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | post; follow and unfollow; read the home feed page by page |
| Non-functional | feed p99 under 200 ms; a new post visible to followers within seconds (not instantly); feed reads matter more than post writes |
| Out of scope | ML ranking (keep it reverse-chronological with light boosts), ads, search |
```text
users        100 M daily active
reads        10 feed loads / user / day = 1 B / day   ≈ 11,600 / s average, ~35,000 / s peak
posts        0.5 / user / day = 50 M / day            ≈ 580 / s average
followers    300 on average, a long tail up to tens of millions
Reads outnumber posts 20 to 1, and the follower counts are wildly uneven. Both facts decide the design.

steps.prompt: If every post is copied into each follower's precomputed timeline, how many timeline inserts per second is that on average?
steps.explain: 580 posts a second become 174,000 small writes a second. That is a lot, but they are cheap list pushes into a cache like Redis, spread over many shards, and they happen in the background.

steps.title: Fan-out on write versus fan-out on read
body: ```text
FAN-OUT ON WRITE (push)                         FAN-OUT ON READ (pull)
post --> posts DB                              post --> posts DB (author's list)
--> fan-out workers --> timeline of       read --> list who I follow (300)
follower 1, 2, ... 300                     --> fetch recent posts of each
read --> one list read: my timeline                --> merge newest first
cheap reads, expensive writes                  cheap writes, expensive reads
- **Push** precomputes each user's timeline (a capped list of post ids, say the latest 800) in a cache. A read is
one key lookup plus hydration. A post by someone with 20 M followers means 20 M inserts.
- **Pull** stores only each author's own posts. A read fans out to everyone you follow and merges, every time.
Following 2,000 accounts means 2,000 lookups per page.
Timelines store **ids**, not posts: an edit or delete then shows up everywhere, and the lists stay small.

items: A feed read is a single list lookup
A post by a huge account creates millions of writes
Inactive users' timelines are built and never read
Every page load merges posts from all followed accounts
Posting is one write, whatever the follower count
Read latency grows with the number of accounts you follow

steps.title: The hybrid: push for most, pull for celebrities
body: Real systems mix both. Pick a **threshold** (say 1 M followers):
- Authors **under** it: push. Their posts go into followers' timelines in the background.
- Authors **over** it: do not push. At read time, fetch their recent posts and merge them into the page.
A user follows maybe a handful of huge accounts, so the read-time merge stays small, and no single post
triggers millions of writes. Two more tricks: only push to followers who were **active recently** (rebuild a
dormant user's timeline on their next visit), and cap each timeline's length.
Order the merge by `(created_at, post_id)`, both descending. The id breaks ties, so the order is total and the
next page can start exactly where this one ended.

prompt: **Symptom first.** An account with 30 M followers posts at 19:00. Your fan-out dashboard:
```text
fan-out queue lag     2 s  ->  41 min
timeline cache CPU    35%  ->  92%
feed reads p99        90 ms -> 640 ms
posts by others       visible after 40+ minutes
What is the best fix?
options: Stop pushing posts of accounts above a follower threshold; merge them in at read time
Add fan-out workers until 30 M inserts finish in a minute
Switch everyone to fan-out on read
steps.explain: One post queued 30 M inserts ahead of everyone else's, and saturated the timeline cache that reads depend on. More workers would only hit the cache harder. Pull-only for everyone makes every read expensive. The hybrid is why it exists.

steps.title: Cursor pagination, not offsets
body: `?offset=40&limit=20` breaks on a live feed: new posts arrive at the top, everything shifts down, and the next
page repeats posts the user just saw. It also makes the server skip 40 items every time.
Use a **cursor**: the sort key of the last item returned.
```text
GET /feed?limit=20                          -> 20 posts, nextCursor = "1764235200:98123"
GET /feed?limit=20&cursor=1764235200:98123  -> posts strictly older than (ts 1764235200, id 98123)
Encode it opaquely (base64) so clients do not build their own. New posts that arrived meanwhile appear when
the user pulls to refresh, not in the middle of their scroll.

steps.prompt: Put the hybrid read path in order.
lines: Read the user's precomputed timeline and the list of huge accounts they follow
Fetch the recent posts of those huge accounts from their own post lists
Merge both lists newest first, after the cursor, dropping duplicates
Hydrate the page's post ids into full posts from the post cache
Return the page and a cursor made from its last item

steps.title: What does the hybrid save?
prompt: For one batch of posts, given each author's follower count, write:
- `long TimelineWrites(int[] followerCounts, int threshold)`: inserts caused by pushing. Authors with **fewer**
followers than `threshold` push one insert per follower; the others push nothing.
- `int PulledAuthors(int[] followerCounts, int threshold)`: how many authors are at or above the threshold
(merged at read time instead).
Careful: the sum can be bigger than an `int`.
solution: int PulledAuthors(int[] followerCounts, int threshold) => followerCounts.Count(f => f >= threshold);
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("with a 1 M threshold only small authors push", 500L, TimelineWrites(dojoBatch, 1_000_000));
Dojo.Eq("two authors are pulled", 2, PulledAuthors(dojoBatch, 1_000_000));
Dojo.Eq("push for everyone", 17_000_500L, TimelineWrites(dojoBatch, int.MaxValue));
Dojo.Eq("nobody pulled", 0, PulledAuthors(dojoBatch, int.MaxValue));
Dojo.Eq("the threshold itself is pulled", 1, PulledAuthors(new[] { 1_000_000 }, 1_000_000));
Dojo.Eq("no int overflow", 4_000_000_000L, TimelineWrites(new[] { 2_000_000_000, 2_000_000_000 }, int.MaxValue));

steps.title: Merge timelines with a cursor
prompt: Write `List<Post> Page(List<List<Post>> timelines, Cursor? after, int limit)`. The template declares
`record Post(long Id, long Ts)` and `record Cursor(long Ts, long Id)`.
- Each list is already sorted newest first: by `Ts` descending, then `Id` descending.
- Return up to `limit` posts in that same order, merged from all lists.
- Only posts strictly **after** the cursor in that order: `Ts < after.Ts`, or the same `Ts` with `Id < after.Id`.
A `null` cursor means start from the top.
- A post can appear in several lists (pushed and pulled): return it once.
A heap-based k-way merge (`PriorityQueue`) only touches what it returns, which matters when the lists are long.
Concatenating and sorting also passes the tests.
starter: List<Post> Page(List<List<Post>> timelines, Cursor? after, int limit)
solution: List<Post> Page(List<List<Post>> timelines, Cursor? after, int limit)
bool Older(Post p) => after is null || p.Ts < after.Ts || (p.Ts == after.Ts && p.Id < after.Id);
var heap = new PriorityQueue<(int L, int I), (long Ts, long Id)>(
Comparer<(long Ts, long Id)>.Create((a, b) => a.Ts != b.Ts ? b.Ts.CompareTo(a.Ts) : b.Id.CompareTo(a.Id)));
while (page.Count < limit && heap.TryDequeue(out var at, out _))
hints: Simple version: `timelines.SelectMany(t => t)`, keep the ones after the cursor, `DistinctBy(p => p.Id)`, order by `Ts` then `Id` descending, `Take(limit)`.
Heap version: enqueue the first post after the cursor from each list with priority `(Ts, Id)` and a comparer that puts larger first; pop, add, push that list's next post.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoA = new List<Post> { new(9, 900), new(6, 600), new(2, 200) };
var dojoB = new List<Post> { new(8, 800), new(6, 600), new(3, 300) };
var dojoC = new List<Post> { new(7, 700), new(5, 600) };
var dojoAll = new List<List<Post>> { dojoA, dojoB, dojoC };
Dojo.Eq("first page, newest first", new List<Post> { new(9, 900), new(8, 800), new(7, 700), new(6, 600) }, Page(dojoAll, null, 4));
Dojo.Eq("next page after (600, 6): the tie at 600 is broken by id", new List<Post> { new(5, 600), new(3, 300), new(2, 200) }, Page(dojoAll, new Cursor(600, 6), 4));
Dojo.Eq("a post pushed and pulled shows once", 7, Page(dojoAll, null, 100).Count);
Dojo.Eq("nothing after the oldest post", new List<Post>(), Page(dojoAll, new Cursor(200, 2), 4));
Dojo.Eq("no timelines, no posts", new List<Post>(), Page(new List<List<Post>>(), null, 4));
record Post(long Id, long Ts);
record Cursor(long Ts, long Id);

steps.title: Build it: the celebrity key
prompt: Celebrities hurt reads too: everyone fetches the same post. In the **System design board**, one key takes half of
all reads from minute three. Find out why adding cache nodes does not help, then fix it so the hottest cache node
stays under its utilisation goal.
steps.explain: A key lives on one node, so a hot key is limited by one node's capacity however big the cluster is. Copies closer to the caller (an in-process near cache) are the fix.
